name: IOIs (indicators of interest)

card.summary: The behaviours (eye contact, smiles, touch, conversation effort) read as signs that someone is attracted, used in looksmaxxing circles as a feedback signal for whether appearance changes are landing.
card.aka: iois, indicators of interest, signals of interest
card.note: Research finds that people often misread subtle interest cues; interpretations in forums are anecdotal.

quick.overview:
IOIs are the small signals people read as meaning someone is interested in them: sustained eye contact, smiling, leaning in, hair or object touching, finding reasons to talk. In looksmaxxing communities the term comes up as a kind of real-world scoreboard, and members swap accounts of how many signals they notice before and after changing their grooming, fitness or style.

The topic links appearance to social feedback. Members treat a shift in attention as a sign that a haircut, fitness change or skin improvement is registering, while others dispute that individual cues can be read reliably. Published research on flirting describes cues such as glances and touch, and also reports that subtle interest is often missed or misread.
quick.how: In practice people observe how strangers and acquaintances respond to them in public, sometimes keeping a mental or written tally, and compare how that changes over time. Guides shared in the forums describe cues to look for and how to respond. Communities also discuss deliberately going out to see whether attention changes.
quick.risks: The main practical issue described in research is misinterpretation: friendliness can be mistaken for romantic interest, and covert interest can go unnoticed. Forum members also describe disappointment when counting signals becomes a measure of self-worth, and some argue the concept leads people to over-read ordinary behaviour.

lead: IOIs, short for indicators of interest, are the verbal and nonverbal signals that someone is interested in another person romantically or sexually. The term circulates widely in dating advice and in looksmaxxing forums, where it is used both as a skill (reading signals) and as a measure (whether changes to appearance produce more of them).

The behaviours usually listed correspond to those described in research on flirting: exchanged glances, smiling, touching, and attentive conversation [1]. Wikipedia's overview of flirting cites studies reporting that greater physical attraction predicts more flirting [1], and that interest is often expressed covertly because overt interest carries social costs [1].
On looksmax.org, threads range from members describing how many IOIs they receive, to guides to interpreting them, to members who dispute that the concept is useful at all [2][3][4][5].

chain: Others respond with more eye contact, smiles and conversation
Member reads the change in attention as feedback on how the look is landing
angle.text: Members use IOIs as an informal read on how their appearance is being received, comparing the attention they get before and after changes. The research literature on flirting describes the cues themselves and how easily they are misjudged.

paras: An indicator of interest is any behaviour taken as a sign of attraction. Wikipedia's article on flirting defines flirting as social communication, through body language, speech or writing, that signals playful interest and possibly romantic or sexual intent, and distinguishes it from simple friendliness [1]. Cues listed there include exchanged glances, hand touching and hair touching [1].
Cultural norms for distance, eye contact and touch vary, so the same behaviour can carry different meanings in different settings [1].

Researchers cited in the flirting literature report several patterns. Greater physical attraction predicted more flirting in a 2000 study by Messman and colleagues [1]. Henningsen and colleagues (2004) found sexually motivated flirting more prominent among men and relationship-building flirting more common among women [1]. Gersick and Kurzban (2014) argued that flirting is often covert because open interest has social costs, and ambiguity preserves deniability [1].
On accuracy, Abbey (1982) found that men sometimes perceive women's friendliness as flirting, and Hall, Xing and Brooks (2015) reported that covert flirting often goes undetected [1].
No studies found. Research on flirting and courtship signalling in social psychology, summarised above, is a related literature rather than a study of IOIs as the forum term uses it.

Forum threads treat IOIs both as evidence of attractiveness and as a contested idea. Some members describe receiving many obvious signals during periods when they were focused on grooming and fitness, and fewer when they stopped [5]. Others post guides to flirting that frame cues scientifically [3] or describe going out to see whether they get attention [6].

A skeptical strand argues that IOIs are over-interpreted, with members saying that reading eye contact or glances is unreliable and that direct conversation is more informative [2][4]. Because these are personal accounts and opinion threads, they describe how members interpret events rather than measured outcomes.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org IOIs are discussed as a way to gauge attractiveness, and also as a concept some members reject [2][3][4][5].

claims.claim: Getting more IOIs shows that your looks are improving
claims.believers: Members describe receiving more signals after improving grooming and fitness and fewer when they let routines lapse [5][6].
claims.experts: Flirting research reports that attraction predicts flirting [1], but also that cues are ambiguous and frequently misread [1]. No study has tested IOI counts as a measure of attractiveness changes.

claims.claim: IOIs do not exist, or cannot be reliably read
claims.believers: Some members argue that signals such as eye contact are over-interpreted, and that attractive men may see people avoid eye contact rather than seek it [2][4].
claims.experts: Published work describes covert flirting that often goes undetected and friendliness mistaken for flirting, which supports ambiguity of cues [1].
